Instead, genuine reliability gain is identified by bootstrap-internal consistency: if the panel's error is stable under resampling of items while the expert's error fluctuates, the panel has genuine (variance-driven) reliability without needing to decompose bias.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the evaluation has too few items for stable bootstrap estimates, the variance comparison is unreliable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert is also highly consistent (low variance), the bootstrap test is null and cannot distinguish the estimators.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the panel's low variance is paired with high bias (e.g., always wrong in the same way), lower variance alone does not prove reliability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The bias-variance decomposition (SCR_002) is elegant but requires knowing the true function to separate bias from variance empirically. A single evaluation lacks this. However, error variance CAN be estimated via bootstrap resampling of cases: if the panel's accuracy is stable under resampling but the expert's is not, the panel has lower variance. If the panel's MEAN error is also not elevated relative to the expert, the gain is genuine. This sidesteps the oracle problem.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
